ap_microeconomics-m01.stem: After a city doubles the price of parking downtown, shoppers switch to the bus, and a bakery sells a bit fewer loaves to shoppers. Which concept best describes why parking demand falls when its price rises?

options.text: The law of demand: at a higher price, consumers buy a smaller quantity and look for substitutes such as the bus.
options.why: A higher price lowers the quantity demanded, and substitutes (bus rides) make the response larger.

options.text: The law of supply: producers offer a smaller quantity at a higher price.
options.why: The law of supply describes sellers' behavior, not shoppers' reaction to a price increase.

options.text: The income effect only, because shoppers have less money after the higher parking price.
options.why: A price change affects quantity demanded through both substitution and income effects; the question points to switching to substitutes.

options.text: Price ceilings, because the city controls the price of parking.
options.why: A price ceiling holds a price below equilibrium; here the city raises the price.

options.text: An increase in demand for the bus that is caused by the parking price, with no change in the quantity of parking demanded.
options.why: The quantity of parking demanded falls along the demand curve; this option ignores the movement.

ap_microeconomics-m01.stem: A town has one vacant lot. The council can use it for a playground or for a parking garage but not both. Which basic economic concept does the council's situation best illustrate?

options.text: A shortage, because the quantity of parking demanded exceeds the quantity supplied at the current price.
options.why: A shortage is a market imbalance at a given price; the council's problem is a limited resource with competing uses.

options.text: Comparative advantage, because the council must specialize in one of the two uses.
options.why: Comparative advantage concerns lower opportunity costs of producers, not a choice between two uses of one resource.

options.text: A market failure, because the lot is not being sold in a competitive market.
options.why: A market failure is an inefficient market outcome; the situation describes a choice under limited resources.

options.text: Diminishing marginal utility, because the lot's value falls with each additional use.
options.why: Nothing in the situation involves the falling value of additional units of one good.

options.text: Scarcity, because the limited resource (land) cannot satisfy both wants, so the council must choose.
options.why: A fixed amount of land with competing uses is a direct example of scarcity, which forces a choice.

ap_microeconomics-m02.stem: A skilled lawyer is also the fastest typist in her office. She hires an assistant to type her documents even though she types faster than the assistant. Which statement best explains why this decision is efficient?

options.text: She has a comparative advantage in legal work, because the opportunity cost of an hour spent typing (the legal work she gives up) is greater than the assistant's.
options.why: Specializing where the opportunity cost is lowest raises total output even if she has an absolute advantage in both tasks.

options.text: She has an absolute advantage in legal work only, because she is better at law than the assistant.
options.why: The lawyer is faster at typing too, so she has an absolute advantage in both tasks; the efficient choice rests on opportunity cost.

options.text: She has a comparative advantage in typing, because she types faster than the assistant.
options.why: Typing faster shows an absolute advantage; the assistant's opportunity cost of typing is lower.

options.text: The decision is efficient only if the assistant is paid less than the lawyer earns for one hour of legal work.
options.why: The decision is efficient whenever the opportunity cost of her typing time exceeds the assistant's, which does not depend on a particular wage comparison alone.

options.text: The decision is inefficient, because she could do both tasks faster herself.
options.why: Doing both tasks herself would give up the more valuable legal work, so total output would be lower.

facts: variant=A skilled lawyer is also the fastest typ

ap_microeconomics-m02.stem: Country X can produce both cars and wheat using fewer resources than Country Z can, so X has an absolute advantage in both goods. Which statement correctly explains whether trade between X and Z can still benefit both countries?

options.text: No, because Country X can make everything more cheaply and would gain nothing from trade.
options.why: Confuses absolute advantage with comparative advantage; gains come from differences in opportunity cost.

options.text: Yes, because each country should produce the good for which its absolute cost of production is lowest.
options.why: Specialization is based on the lowest opportunity cost, not the lowest absolute resource cost.

options.text: No, because trade is beneficial only when each country has an absolute advantage in a different good.
options.why: Absolute advantage in different goods is not required; comparative advantage is enough.

options.text: Yes, but only Country Z gains, because the country with the absolute advantage gives up nothing.
options.why: Country X also gains by concentrating on the good for which its opportunity cost is lower and importing the other.

options.text: Yes, because gains from trade depend on comparative advantage: each country should specialize in the good for which its opportunity cost is lower.
options.why: Even a country with an absolute advantage in everything has a lower opportunity cost in only one good, so both can gain by specializing and trading.
